body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.intro.0: The urban heat island — the excess of air and land surface temperature in a city over the surrounding rural area — is one of the most extensively studied manifestations of anthropogenic climate transformation. Classic studies attribute this phenomenon to changes in the heat balance: the replacement of vegetation with impervious surfaces reduces evaporation, the geometry of the built environment diminishes nocturnal radiative cooling, and anthropogenic sources add heat to the surface layer.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.intro.1: The overwhelming majority of empirical estimates, however, have been obtained for cities with populations of over one million. Medium-sized cities with 100–500 thousand inhabitants are often regarded as “too small” to develop a pronounced heat island, even though it is precisely in such cities that active construction on the periphery has been observed over the past two decades. The present study fills this gap: we estimate the intensity of the surface heat island in twelve medium-sized cities and identify the factors behind its change over 2000–2023.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.methods.0: The study covers twelve cities of the temperate zone, designated in the article by the codes C1–C12. For each city, cloud-free scenes for June–August were selected from the Landsat archive (on average 4.6 scenes per city per year, 1,318 scenes in total). Land surface temperature was retrieved from the thermal band with an NDVI-based emissivity correction.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.methods.1: Heat island intensity (HII) was defined as the difference between the median temperature of the built-up area and that of a 5 km wide suburban buffer ring, excluding water bodies. Mean NDVI, the share of impervious surfaces, building density and population size were used as explanatory variables. The relationship was estimated with a mixed-effects regression model with a random intercept for city and a fixed effect for year.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.results.0: The mean daytime HII across the whole sample was 3.4 ± 0.8 °C. The lowest values are characteristic of cities with a well-developed valley network and preserved forest parks (2.1–2.6 °C), and the highest of cities in the steppe zone with dense prefabricated panel housing (4.5–4.9 °C). Fig. 1 shows the dynamics of mean intensity by five-year periods.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.results.1: In the regression model (Table 1), NDVI has the largest effect: a decrease in the index by 0.1 is associated with an increase in HII of 0.62 °C. The share of impervious surfaces is significant, but its effect is largely mediated by vegetation. Population size is statistically insignificant once morphological indicators are taken into account.

body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.discussion.0: The intensity estimates obtained are comparable with those published for European cities of similar size and are only 1–1.5 °C lower than the values for the largest agglomerations. This calls into question the widespread notion that heat risk in medium-sized cities is negligible.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.discussion.1: The most important finding of the study is the leading role of vegetation on the periphery. New residential neighbourhoods built after 2010 on former agricultural land and wasteland have minimal green cover, and it is here that the increase in surface temperature is most pronounced. A limitation of the study is the use of daytime scenes only: the nocturnal heat island, which is the most significant for health, requires other data sources.
body.v1n1-01-urban-heat.conclusion.0: Medium-sized cities develop pronounced surface heat islands whose intensity is increasing. Preserving and creating green spaces in areas of new development is the most effective lever for adaptation. The proposed open algorithm can be used by municipalities for monitoring.
body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.intro.0: Fine particulate matter PM2.5 is one of the main health risk factors associated with ambient air pollution. Reference monitoring stations are expensive and few in number: a typical city with a population of half a million has one or two of them. Low-cost optical sensors costing a few thousand roubles make it possible to build a dense network, but their readings require calibration.
body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.intro.1: The main source of error is the hygroscopic growth of particles at high humidity, which causes the sensor to overestimate mass concentration. In a sharply continental climate, low winter temperatures that affect the performance of the electronics add to this. The aim of the study is to compare calibration methods and to assess their transferability between seasons.
body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.methods: Eight sensors of the same model were installed on the roof of the reference station shelter at a height of 3 m. The observation period ran from October 2022 to November 2023. The data were aggregated to hourly values; hours with incomplete records (less than 45 minutes) were excluded. The final sample comprised 76,412 pairs of observations.

Four models were compared: simple linear regression on the raw signal; multiple regression with relative humidity, temperature and their interaction; random forest (500 trees); and gradient boosting (depth 6, learning rate 0.05). Performance was assessed using blocked cross-validation: the data were split into weekly blocks, and each block in turn served as the test set.
body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.results: The results of the comparison are presented in Table 1 and Fig. 1. All calibration methods substantially reduce the error; the difference between humidity-corrected linear regression and the ensemble methods is particularly large at relative humidity above 80%.

When trained on summer data only and tested on winter data, the mean absolute error of gradient boosting rose to 7.9 µg/m³, which is only slightly better than linear correction. Adding even one winter month to the training set reduced the error to 3.6 µg/m³.

body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.discuss: The post-calibration error values obtained are comparable with the tolerances for indicative measurements and allow a network of low-cost sensors to be used for estimating diurnal profiles and identifying local sources — boiler houses, highways and private housing with stove heating.

The lack of seasonal transferability of the models is an important practical limitation. A calibration performed in summer may produce systematic errors in winter, when pollution is most hazardous. We recommend a co-location period of at least one year before deploying a network.
body.v1n1-02-air-quality-sensors.conclus: Ensemble machine learning methods reduce the error of low-cost PM2.5 sensors almost fourfold. The key condition for correct calibration is that the training set includes data from all seasons of the year.
